method: Lectio Edition (SDIT): clear modern English of the Tao Te Ching, synthesized from the public-domain translation tradition (James Legge 1891; Arthur Waley 1934 consulted, not quoted) and checked against the Classical Chinese; modern translations consulted, not quoted. In progress, chapter by chapter.
sourcesCited: Classical Chinese, the original text of the Daodejing
James Legge, The Tâo Teh King (1891, Sacred Books of the East, public domain)
Walter Gorn Old, The Book of the Simple Way (1904, public domain)
D. C. Lau (1963, consulted, not quoted)
overview: The Lectio Edition renders the Tao Te Ching in clear modern English that keeps the paradox and quiet authority of the eighty-one chapters — the Way that cannot be named, the power that works by yielding, the sage who leads by stepping back — while shedding the knotty Victorian diction of the older scholarly versions.
introduction: The Tao Te Ching is a slim book of eighty-one short chapters, by turns poem and proverb, ascribed to the sage Lao Tzu. It teaches the Tao — the Way — that underlies all things and cannot be captured in words, and the te, the quiet power of acting without forcing (wu wei). Read it a chapter at a time; it is meant to be returned to, not finished.

divergences.phrase: The Way that can be spoken is not the eternal Way.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao."
divergences.lectio: The Way that can be spoken is not the eternal Way.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 道可道，非常道. The second 道 (dào) is a verb, and in the oldest usage it means "to speak" or "to put into words." Legge read it as "to tread" (a path one can walk), which is grammatically possible but loses the chapter's real argument — that the Way which can be captured in language is not the true, lasting Way. The whole opening turns on speaking and naming, so we keep "spoken," the reading nearly all modern scholars share.

divergences.phrase: Nameless, it is the origin of heaven and earth. Named, it is the mother of all things.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "(Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things."
divergences.lectio: Nameless, it is the origin of heaven and earth. Named, it is the mother of all things.
divergences.note: Legge's bracketed "(conceived of as)" is honest scholarship — the Chinese (無名天地之始；有名萬物之母) leaves the grammar open — but it clutters the line. We drop the scaffolding and let the bare contrast stand, which is how the original reads: nameless at the source, named as things take form.

divergences.phrase: mystery within mystery, the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Together we call them the Mystery. Where the Mystery is the deepest is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful."
divergences.lectio: Together they are the Mystery — mystery within mystery, the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.
divergences.note: The Chinese 玄之又玄 is literally "dark, and again dark" — mystery folded inside mystery. Legge flattened this into "where the Mystery is the deepest," smoothing the doubling away. We keep the repetition (玄, xuán, dark/mysterious) because the chapter ends by deepening, not measuring; that recursive dark opens onto 眾妙之門, the gate of all wonders.

divergences.phrase: When everyone in the world recognizes beauty as beauty, ugliness has already appeared
divergences.older: All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what ugliness is (Legge 1891)
divergences.lectio: When everyone in the world recognizes beauty as beauty, ugliness has already appeared
divergences.note: The Chinese (天下皆知美之為美，斯惡已) is tighter and more unsettling than Legge's gloss: the very act of naming beauty calls its opposite into being. We render the opposites as plain pairs and keep the paradox bare, dropping Legge's parenthetical '(the idea of)' so the line lands as the original does — to define one thing is to create the other.

divergences.phrase: the sage goes about the work without forcing it
divergences.older: the sage manages affairs without doing anything (Legge 1891)
divergences.lectio: the sage goes about the work without forcing it
divergences.note: This is wu wei (為無為 / 無為), the book's central paradox. Legge's 'without doing anything' reads as idleness, which misses the point — the sage is fully engaged but never strains against the grain of things. We render it as acting-without-forcing: action that does not impose, so the work still gets done.

divergences.phrase: It is just because he does not rest in it that the credit never leaves him
divergences.older: The work is done, but how no one can see; 'Tis this that makes the power not cease to be (Legge 1891)
divergences.lectio: It is just because he does not rest in it that the credit never leaves him
divergences.note: Legge turns the closing line (夫唯弗居，是以不去) into a rhyming couplet of his own. The Chinese is a single conditional turn: precisely because the sage takes no credit, the credit is never lost to him. We keep that logic plain — the reward of yielding is that nothing has to be defended, so nothing slips away.

divergences.phrase: 為無為，則無不治
divergences.older: When there is this abstinence from action, good order is universal. (Legge, 1891)
divergences.lectio: Act without forcing, and nothing is left ungoverned.
divergences.note: Legge turns the line into mere 'abstinence from action,' but the Chinese is the active paradox wei wu-wei — literally 'do the not-doing.' It is not idleness; it is acting without straining against the grain of things (wu wei). We keep it as a positive command so the paradox stands.

divergences.phrase: 弱其志，強其骨
divergences.older: weakens their wills, and strengthens their bones (Legge, 1891)
divergences.lectio: weakens their ambition and strengthens their bones
divergences.note: The word zhi is the striving, grasping drive — not the faculty of will as such. 'Ambition' catches what Laozi means: the restless wanting that breeds rivalry and theft in the opening lines. He would quiet that craving while keeping the body sound and well-fed.

divergences.phrase: empty, yet never used up
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel; and in our employment of it we must be on our guard against all fulness."
divergences.lectio: The Way is empty, yet however much you use it, it is never used up.
divergences.note: The Chinese 道沖而用之或不盈 turns on chong (沖), the hollow emptiness of a vessel, and bu ying (不盈), "never filled / never overflows." Legge reads it as a moral caution to guard against fullness; most readers since take it as a statement about the Way itself — its emptiness is precisely what makes it inexhaustible. We follow the plainer reading and keep the paradox: empty, yet never used up.

divergences.phrase: the wellspring from which the ten thousand things flow
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things!"
divergences.lectio: the wellspring from which the ten thousand things flow
divergences.note: The text reads wan wu zhi zong (萬物之宗) — literally the "ancestor" or clan-source of the ten thousand things — paired with yuan (淵), a deep pool or abyss. Legge's "Honoured Ancestor" is faithful but stiff; we keep the image of depth alive by rendering zong as a wellspring or source, the deep place everything pours out of, while preserving "the ten thousand things," the classic Chinese phrase for all that exists.

divergences.phrase: older than God
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "It might appear to have been before God."
divergences.lectio: It seems to be older than God.
divergences.note: The closing line xiang di zhi xian (象帝之先) says the Way seems (xiang, 象) to come before Di (帝) — the high god, the Lord on High of ancient Chinese religion, whom Legge renders "God." The startling claim is deliberate: even the highest divine ruler is not first; the Way is older still. We preserve it exactly — "older than God" — rather than softening Di to an abstraction, since the shock is the point.

divergences.phrase: straw dogs (芻狗)
divergences.older: the dogs of grass (Legge); the grass-dogs (Old)
divergences.lectio: straw dogs
divergences.note: A straw dog was a figure of bound straw made for a sacrifice: handled with great care and honor while the rite was on, then thrown away and trampled the moment it was over — no cruelty in it, just the natural end of its use. Heaven and earth treat all things this way: not with malice, but without favoritism or sentiment. Legge's 'the dogs of grass' is literal but opaque to a modern reader; we keep the now-standard 'straw dogs' and let the image carry the chapter's hardest point.

divergences.phrase: not humane (不仁)
divergences.older: do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be benevolent (Legge)
divergences.lectio: are not humane
divergences.note: Ren (仁) is the great Confucian virtue — humaneness, human-heartedness, the warm partiality of treating people as your own. Laozi deliberately denies it of heaven and earth, and of the sage who imitates them: they are not ren. The point is not that nature is cruel but that it plays no favorites; its impartiality can look like indifference. We render ren as 'humane' here to match the Lectio Analects edition (which renders ren as 'humaneness'), so the reader can hear Laozi answering Confucius. Legge's unpacked 'any wish to be benevolent' dilutes the deliberate shock of the bare 'not humane.'

divergences.locus: Chapter 5, bellows lines (虛而不屈，動而愈出)
divergences.phrase: empty, yet it never runs out
divergences.older: 'Tis emptied, yet it loses not its power (Legge)
divergences.lectio: Empty, yet it never runs out; work it, and it gives out all the more
divergences.note: The Chinese (虛而不屈, 動而愈出) describes a bellows: hollow inside, yet it never gives out, and the more you pump it the more wind it sends. The emptiness is the source of the inexhaustible supply — a core Taoist paradox. Legge's verse ('loses not its power') is accurate but Victorian; we keep the plain mechanism of the bellows so the paradox — emptiness as fullness — lands directly. 'Keep to the center' (守中) at the close echoes this same hollow center that does not run dry.

divergences.phrase: the valley spirit
divergences.older: The valley spirit dies not, aye the same (Legge 1891)
divergences.lectio: The valley spirit never dies.
divergences.note: The Chinese gushen joins gu, the empty hollow of a valley, to shen, spirit. The valley is the open, low, receptive space that is never filled and never depleted; its spirit is the inexhaustible life of that emptiness. We keep the literal 'valley spirit' rather than smoothing it to an abstraction, since the image of the hollow that gives without running dry is the whole point.

divergences.phrase: the mysterious female
divergences.older: The female mystery thus do we name (Legge 1891)
divergences.lectio: It is called the mysterious female. The gateway of the mysterious female is called the root of heaven and earth.
divergences.note: Xuanpin pairs xuan, dark or mysterious, with pin, the female of an animal, the bearing and birthing power. The chapter names a generative source from which all things come, its 'gateway' the root of heaven and earth. We hold to 'the mysterious female' rather than softening it to 'divine feminine' or dropping the strangeness; the dark, fertile, opening power is the chapter's central figure.

divergences.phrase: they do not live for themselves, and so they go on living
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "because they do not live of, or for, themselves. This is how they are able to continue and endure."
divergences.lectio: they do not live for themselves, and so they go on living
divergences.note: The Chinese 以其不自生，故能長生 turns on a single paradox: bu zi sheng (不自生) — not living for, or out of, themselves — is exactly what grants chang sheng (長生), long life. Legge's doubled "of, or for" hedges the grammar honestly, and his closing sentence restates the cause flatly. We let the paradox stand bare as one turn: precisely by not living for themselves, heaven and earth go on living. The self-forgetting is the source of the endurance, and that pivot reaches forward into the sage's selflessness in the second half.

divergences.locus: closing line (非以其無私邪？故能成其私)
divergences.phrase: Is it not because he is selfless that his own self is fulfilled?
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Is it not because he has no personal and private ends, that therefore such ends are realised?"
divergences.lectio: Is it not because he is selfless that his own self is fulfilled?
divergences.note: The Chinese 非以其無私邪？故能成其私 pivots on the same word, si (私), the private self, used twice: it is by having no si (無私, selflessness) that the sage cheng qi si (成其私), completes or fulfills his self. Legge unpacks si into "personal and private ends," which is faithful but loses the sting of the single repeated word. We keep the bare echo — selfless, yet his self fulfilled — so the closing paradox lands as sharply in English as it does in the Chinese: the one who seeks nothing for himself is the one who is made whole.

divergences.phrase: The highest good is like water.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The highest excellence is like (that of) water."
divergences.lectio: The highest good is like water.
divergences.note: The Chinese 上善若水 reads literally "highest good is like water." Legge's "excellence" is faithful but stiff, and his bracketed "(that of)" clutters the line. Shan (善) is the same word the chapter then repeats down its list of virtues; we keep it as "good" so the reader hears one idea — the good that, like water, gives without grasping — carried straight through the chapter.

divergences.phrase: Water benefits all things and does not contend with them; it settles in the low places that everyone else scorns.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike."
divergences.lectio: Water benefits all things and does not contend with them; it settles in the low places that everyone else scorns.
divergences.note: The line is 水善利萬物而不爭，處眾人之所惡. The verb 爭 (zhēng) is "to contend, to compete, to push against" — the same word that returns in the chapter's closing line, where it must be "contend" for the argument to land. Legge splits it into "striving" here and "wrangling" at the close, hiding the deliberate echo. We render 爭 as "contend" both times, so the chapter's frame holds: water gains its power precisely by not contending, and so does the sage.

divergences.phrase: In where it dwells, it holds to the ground. In the heart, it holds to depth...
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The excellence of a residence is in (the suitability of) the place; that of the mind is in abysmal stillness..."
divergences.lectio: In where it dwells, it holds to the ground. In the heart, it holds to depth. In giving, it holds to kindness. In speech, it holds to truth. In governing, it holds to good order. In handling affairs, it holds to skill. In moving, it holds to the right moment.
divergences.note: The Chinese is a tight chant of seven matched clauses (居善地，心善淵，與善仁，言善信，正善治，事善能，動善時), each pairing a domain of life with the kind of goodness proper to it — and each repeating shan (善), "good," the word that opened the chapter. Legge unrolls them into long abstract phrases ("the suitability of the place," "abysmal stillness") that break the rhythm and lose the drumbeat of the repeated word. We keep the parallel form and the recurring "holds to," so the list reads as it sounds in Chinese: a steady, water-like settling of each thing into its true place.

divergences.phrase: Hammer a blade to its sharpest edge, and the edge will not last.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness."
divergences.lectio: Hammer a blade to its sharpest edge, and the edge will not last.
divergences.note: The Chinese 揣而銳之 pairs chuai (揣), to pound or hammer out, with rui (銳), to sharpen to a point — the smith working a blade to its keenest edge. Legge's "keep feeling a point" misreads the act as testing the tip rather than over-honing it, and his Victorian phrasing obscures the image. We restore the forge: push the edge past its limit and it cannot hold, the same lesson as the overfilled cup.

divergences.phrase: When the work is done and your name is rising, withdraw. This is the Way of heaven.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven."
divergences.lectio: When the work is done and your name is rising, withdraw. This is the Way of heaven.
divergences.note: The Chinese 功遂身退 is spare — "the deed accomplished, the self steps back" — and 天之道 names it the Way of heaven. Legge's "withdraw into obscurity" adds a self-erasing dimness the text does not carry; the point is timely retreat at the height of success, not vanishing. We keep the bare gesture of stepping back and preserve "the Way of heaven," since the chapter closes by naming this knowing-when-to-stop as heaven's own pattern.

divergences.phrase: cleanse the dark mirror of your mind until it is without a flaw
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "When he has cleansed away the most mysterious sights (of his imagination), he can become without a flaw."
divergences.lectio: Can you cleanse the dark mirror of your mind until it is without a flaw?
divergences.note: The crux is 滌除玄覽. Legge read 覽 (lǎn, "to view") as the act of seeing and rendered it "the most mysterious sights" — the imagination's visions, to be washed away. But many readers, following the Mawangdui manuscripts where the graph is 鑒/監 (jiàn, "mirror"), take 玄覽 as the xuan jian, the "dark mirror" — the deep, still mind that reflects the world without distortion. The line then asks not that you erase your inner sights but that you polish the mirror of awareness until it shows no smudge. We follow the mirror reading, which keeps the chapter's image of a flawless, undistorting clarity.

divergences.locus: the gate of heaven (天門開闔，能為雌乎)
divergences.phrase: can you keep to the female, the yielding, receptive part
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "In the opening and shutting of his gates of heaven, cannot he do so as a female bird?"
divergences.lectio: When the gate of heaven opens and shuts, can you keep to the female, the yielding, receptive part?
divergences.note: 天門開闔，能為雌乎 asks whether, as the "gate of heaven" opens and closes — the rhythm of action and stillness, coming and going — you can play the part of 雌 (cí), the female. Legge's "as a female bird" is over-literal (雌 is the hen as opposed to the cock) and obscures the point. Throughout the book the female stands for the receptive, yielding power that prevails by softness, not force; here it answers the same motion the male would meet with assertion. We render 雌 as the female, the yielding, receptive part, keeping the gender image that runs through the Way while making its meaning plain.

divergences.locus: the close (生而不有，為而不恃，長而不宰，是謂玄德)
divergences.phrase: this is what is called the mysterious power
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "it produces them and does not claim them as its own; it does all, and yet does not boast of it; it presides over all, and yet does not control them. This is what is called 'The mysterious Quality.'"
divergences.lectio: To give life and not possess it; to do the work and not lay claim to it; to lead, and not to lord it over what you lead — this is what is called the mysterious power.
divergences.note: The chapter closes on 玄德 (xuán dé), literally "dark virtue" — the same xuan, the deep mystery, that opens the book, joined to de, the inner power of the Way. Legge's "mysterious Quality" is faithful but pale. We render de as "power" (the te the book is named for) and keep xuan as "mysterious," so the phrase lands as the book's signature paradox: the power that gives life without owning it, acts without taking credit, leads without mastering — power exactly because it does not grasp. The triad 不有 / 不恃 / 不宰 (does not possess, does not claim, does not lord over) is kept as three plain, parallel refusals.

divergences.phrase: where there is nothing
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends"; Walter Gorn Old (1904): "made useful by the hole in the centre, where nothing exists."
divergences.lectio: it is the hole at the center, where there is nothing, that makes the wheel of use.
divergences.note: Each image turns on the same refrain, 當其無 (dāng qí wú) — "just here, in its nothing." Wu (無) is the book's great word for emptiness, absence, what-is-not. Legge keeps inserting bracketed clarifications — "(for the axle)," "(from the walls)," "(within)" — to pin down where the emptiness sits; honest, but it clutters a line whose whole force is the bare nothing. We let the refrain repeat plainly across all three images (hub, pot, room) so the reader feels the pattern build, the way the Chinese does.

divergences.locus: closing antithesis (有之以為利，無之以為用)
divergences.phrase: what is there gives advantage; what is not there gives use
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "what has a (positive) existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for (actual) usefulness."
divergences.lectio: So what is there gives advantage; what is not there gives use.
divergences.note: The hinge of the chapter is a tight antithesis: 有 (yǒu, having / what is there) gives 利 (lì, advantage, benefit), while 無 (wú, not-having / what is not there) gives 用 (yòng, use, function). Legge's "profitable adaptation" and "(positive) existence" bury a sharp epigram under Victorian abstraction. We keep the two halves balanced and bare — advantage from the solid, use from the void — so the paradox lands as a saying you can carry: the substance is what you pay for, but the emptiness is what you live in.

divergences.phrase: The five flavors numb the palate.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The flavours five deprive the mouth of taste."
divergences.lectio: The five flavors numb the palate.
divergences.note: The Chinese 五味令人口爽 turns on shuang (爽), which here does not mean "refreshed" but its older sense of dulled or spoiled — the palate jaded by too much. Legge's "deprive the mouth of taste" gets the drift, but "numb the palate" keeps the active image: overindulgence does not strip taste away so much as deaden it, the way too many flavors leave the tongue unable to tell anything apart.

divergences.phrase: goods that are hard to come by knock a life off its course
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "objects rare and strange, Sought for, men's conduct will to evil change."
divergences.lectio: goods that are hard to come by knock a life off its course
divergences.note: The Chinese 難得之貨，令人行妨 says that hard-to-get goods cause one's xing (行) — one's conduct, one's walking-through-life — to be fang (妨), obstructed or harmed. Legge moralizes it into conduct changing "to evil," but the text is plainer and more physical: chasing rare things trips you up and throws your course off, the same image of derailment that runs through the chapter's racing and hunting.

divergences.phrase: Favor and disgrace are both alarming.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared."
divergences.lectio: Favor and disgrace are both alarming.
divergences.note: The Chinese 寵辱若驚 is spare: chong (寵, favor) and ru (辱, disgrace) are each ruo jing (若驚) — "as if startled," alarming, a shock to the nerves. Legge's "would seem equally to be feared" hedges with "would seem" and softens jing (the jolt of being startled) into mere "fear." The point is sharper than fear: both favor and disgrace unsettle you, because both put you at the mercy of what others give and take. We keep the bare jolt — both alarming — so the paradox lands: the prize disturbs your peace as much as the shame.

divergences.phrase: The reason I can suffer great trouble is that I have a body.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "What makes me liable to great calamity is my having the body (which I call myself); if I had not the body, what great calamity could come to me?"
divergences.lectio: The reason I can suffer great trouble is that I have a body; if I had no body, what trouble could reach me?
divergences.note: The crux is shen (身), which means both the physical body and the self — what you call "me." The chapter turns on it: you can be honored or harmed only because you have a self to attach to, a body that wins and loses, fears and grasps. Legge's bracketed "(which I call myself)" is honest but clutters the line. We keep shen as "body" throughout, since the chapter's whole argument is that fixing on the self is the root of both the favor you crave and the trouble you dread.

divergences.phrase: the one who honors the world as their own body can be given the world to hold
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "he who would administer the kingdom, honouring it as he honours his own person, may be employed to govern it, and he who would administer it with the love which he bears to his own person may be entrusted with it."
divergences.lectio: So the one who honors the world as their own body can be given the world to hold; the one who loves the world as their own body can be trusted with the world.
divergences.note: The Chinese (貴以身為天下，若可寄天下；愛以身為天下，若可託天下) pairs gui (貴, to honor, hold precious) with ai (愛, to love), and tian xia (天下, "all under heaven") — the world, not just one kingdom. The argument completes the chapter's turn on shen (身, body/self): only someone who treats the world with the same care they give their own body — neither clutching it for favor nor flinching from its troubles — is fit to be entrusted with it. Legge's "administer the kingdom" and "his own person" are faithful but stiff, and narrow tian xia to a single realm. We keep "the world" and the plain body/self echo, so the famous lesson stands clear: power belongs to the one who holds the world as dearly, and as lightly, as their own life.

divergences.locus: the three names (夷, 希, 微)
divergences.phrase: the Unseen ... the Unheard ... the Unfelt
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "we name it 'the Equable' ... we name it 'the Inaudible' ... we name it 'the Subtle.'"
divergences.lectio: Look for it, and you do not see it: call it the Unseen. Listen for it, and you do not hear it: call it the Unheard. Reach for it, and you cannot hold it: call it the Unfelt.
divergences.note: The Chinese names the Way by three failures of the senses: 夷 (yí), paired with 視之不見 — looked for but not seen; 希 (xī), with 聽之不聞 — listened for but not heard; 微 (wēi), with 搏之不得 — grasped for but not held. The three graphs are obscure even in Chinese, which is the point: each names the limit of one sense. Legge's 'the Equable' for 夷 reaches for an etymology (level, even) that breaks the pattern of negation the other two keep. We render all three as plain privatives tied to their sense — Unseen, Unheard, Unfelt — so the parallel that the original builds stands, and the line drives home that the Way slips past every faculty we have to catch it.

divergences.locus: the formless form (無狀之狀，無物之象)
divergences.phrase: the form of the formless, the image of what has no thing in it
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "This is called the Form of the Formless, and the Semblance of the Invisible."
divergences.lectio: This is the form of the formless, the image of what has no thing in it.
divergences.note: The Chinese is a matched pair: 無狀之狀 (wú zhuàng zhī zhuàng), the shape of no-shape, and 無物之象 (wú wù zhī xiàng), the image of no-thing. Legge keeps the first paradox ('Form of the Formless') but smooths the second into 'the Semblance of the Invisible,' losing 物 (wù), the bare word for a thing or object. We hold both halves literal — the form of the formless, the image of what has no thing in it — so the chapter's central riddle lands twice, as the original means it to: a shape with nothing in it to shape, an image of nothing there to picture.

divergences.locus: the thread of the Way (是謂道紀)
divergences.phrase: this is called the thread of the Way
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "this is called (unwinding) the clue of Tao."
divergences.lectio: To know how things were in the beginning long ago — this is called the thread of the Way.
divergences.note: The closing phrase is 道紀 (dào jì). 紀 is the binding thread of a net, the cord that gathers the strands — by extension a discipline, a guiding principle. Legge's '(unwinding) the clue of Tao' uses 'clue' in its old sense of a ball of thread (a clew, as in Theseus's), but to a modern reader 'clue' now means a hint, which misleads. We keep the literal image — the thread of the Way — the single line you hold on to that runs from the ancient beginning straight into the present, letting you master today by keeping hold of what was first.

divergences.phrase: Plain, like an uncarved block of wood.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "unpretentious like wood that has not been fashioned into anything"
divergences.lectio: Plain, like an uncarved block of wood.
divergences.note: The Chinese 樸 (pu) is the unworked log before the carver touches it — Laozi's standing image for original, undivided simplicity, which returns by name in later chapters. Legge's "wood that has not been fashioned into anything" is faithful but loses the noun the tradition itself uses. We keep "the uncarved block," now the standard English term, so the reader meets the same emblem of plainness Laozi builds on throughout the book.

divergences.locus: closing line (夫唯不盈，故能蔽不新成)
divergences.phrase: he can wear out and be made new again
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "It is through their not being full of themselves that they can afford to seem worn and not appear new and complete."
divergences.lectio: because he is never full, he can wear out and be made new again
divergences.note: The crux is 蔽不新成. Legge reads it as seeming "worn and not new and complete" — a kind of contented shabbiness. But many readers take bi (蔽), worn out or covered over, against a renewal that the emptiness makes possible: precisely because he never fills himself up, he can be used up and yet remade. We follow the reading that keeps the chapter's paradox of renewal — the one who is never full is never finished, and so can always be renewed.

divergences.phrase: returning to the root is stillness; this is called returning to what was fated
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "This returning to their root is what we call the state of stillness; and that stillness may be called a reporting that they have fulfilled their appointed end."
divergences.lectio: Returning to the root is stillness; this is called returning to what was fated.
divergences.note: The crux is 復命 (fùmìng). Ming (命) is the decree, the fated nature a thing is given at its origin; fu (復) is to return. The line says that a thing, in coming to rest, goes back to the lot it was assigned — its true, given nature. Legge unfolds ming into "a reporting that they have fulfilled their appointed end," reading it as a creature handing in a report on a task completed. That is one old gloss, but it buries the plain image: the return to the root is a return to one's fate, the still ground one came from. We keep the bare turn so the chapter's circle holds — out from the root, back to the root, which is stillness, which is the given destiny.

divergences.locus: the ladder (知常容，容乃公，公乃王，王乃天，天乃道，道乃久)
divergences.phrase: all-embracing, you are impartial; impartial, you are kingly; kingly, you are like heaven; like heaven, you are one with the Way
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The knowledge of that unchanging rule produces a (grand) capacity and forbearance, and that capacity and forbearance lead to a community (of feeling with all things). From this community of feeling comes a kingliness of character..."
divergences.lectio: Know the constant, and you grow all-embracing. All-embracing, you are impartial; impartial, you are kingly; kingly, you are like heaven; like heaven, you are one with the Way.
divergences.note: The Chinese is a tight ascending chain — 容 (róng, holding all, all-embracing) → 公 (gōng, public, impartial) → 王 (wáng, king) → 天 (tiān, heaven) → 道 (dào, the Way) → 久 (jiǔ, lasting) — each rung lifting off the one before. Legge unrolls it into long abstractions ("capacity and forbearance," "a community of feeling with all things") that break the climb and lose the step-by-step rhythm. We restore the ladder as a series of plain links so the reader feels it rise: knowing the constant opens you wide, and an open heart plays no favorites, and the one who plays no favorites rules, and rule reaches up to heaven, and heaven to the Way, and the Way endures.

divergences.phrase: to the end of your life you come to no harm
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "and to the end of his bodily life, is exempt from all danger of decay."
divergences.lectio: to the end of your life you come to no harm.
divergences.note: The Chinese 沒身不殆 is spare: mò shēn (沒身), "to the sinking of the body," meaning all one's life long to its very end; bù dài (不殆), "no danger, no peril." Legge's "exempt from all danger of decay" adds a notion of decay the words do not carry and stiffens the close. We keep it plain — one with the Way, you last, and you are safe to the last breath — so the chapter ends where it began, in the stillness that does not perish.

divergences.phrase: The best ruler is one the people barely know is there.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "In the highest antiquity, (the people) did not know that there were (their rulers)."
divergences.lectio: The best ruler is one the people barely know is there.
divergences.note: The received Wang Bi text reads 太上，下知有之 — "the best: those below merely know he exists." Legge followed a variant (不知有之, "did not know there were rulers") and folded it into a story about "highest antiquity," the earliest age. But the chapter is not about a lost golden age; it is ranking kinds of rule, best to worst, in the present. We keep the plain comparison — the ideal ruler is the one so light a touch that the people are scarcely aware of him — which is the reading nearly all modern scholars share and which sets up the descending list that follows.

divergences.phrase: the people all say: we did this ourselves.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "the people all said, 'We are as we are, of ourselves!'"
divergences.lectio: the people all say: we did this ourselves.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 百姓皆謂：我自然. The phrase 自然 (zìrán) is the book's great word — "so of itself," what is naturally so without being forced. Legge's "we are as we are, of ourselves" is faithful to that sense of unforced self-arising, but it sounds like a remark about identity rather than about the work just finished. The point is that the ruler's hand was so quiet that, with the task accomplished, the people credit themselves: "we did this ourselves." We keep that ordinary, almost surprised voice, since the whole chapter turns on a ruler who leads by leaving no fingerprints.

divergences.locus: the six kinships (六親不和，有孝慈)
divergences.phrase: filial devotion and parental love are praised
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "When harmony no longer prevailed throughout the six kinships, filial sons found their manifestation."
divergences.lectio: When the six bonds of kin fall out of harmony, filial devotion and parental love are praised.
divergences.note: The Chinese 孝慈 is a pair: xiao (孝), the child's devotion to parents, and ci (慈), the parent's tenderness toward the child. Legge names only the "filial sons," dropping ci and turning the couplet one-sided. We keep both halves, since the chapter's irony depends on it — these warm family virtues become words on everyone's lips only once the natural harmony that made them go without saying has broken down.

divergences.locus: the chapter's irony (大道廢，有仁義)
divergences.phrase: come forward
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed, benevolence and righteousness came into vogue."
divergences.lectio: When the great Way is abandoned, humaneness and righteousness come forward.
divergences.note: The whole chapter turns on a single ironic structure: each named virtue appears only because something was lost. The Chinese has no word for "because," just bare juxtaposition — the Way fails, and there is ren and yi (仁義). We render ren as "humaneness" to match the Lectio Analects edition, so the reader hears Laozi answering Confucius: the great Confucian virtues are not the cure but the symptom. The point is sharpest if the line stays flat and unforced — "come forward," not Legge's dated "came into vogue" — so the virtues sound like names rushing in to fill a hole.

divergences.phrase: Renounce humaneness, throw out righteousness, and the people will return to devotion within their families and care for one another.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "If we could renounce our benevolence and discard our righteousness, the people would again become filial and kindly."
divergences.lectio: Renounce humaneness, throw out righteousness, and the people will return to devotion within their families and care for one another.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 絕仁棄義，民復孝慈. 仁 (rén) is the Confucian virtue of humaneness, which we render throughout the edition as "humaneness" rather than Legge's "benevolence," to keep it consistent with Chapter 18 and to mark it as the named, official virtue Laozi is criticizing. 孝慈 is the pair filial-devotion (孝, child to parent) and parental-love (慈, parent to child); Legge's "filial and kindly" flattens the reciprocity, so we keep both directions: devotion within the family and care for one another.

divergences.phrase: see the plain and undyed, hold to the uncarved block
divergences.older: Legge (1891), in verse: "But simple views, and courses plain and true / Would selfish ends and many lusts eschew."
divergences.lectio: see the plain and undyed, hold to the uncarved block, think little of self, and want little.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 見素抱樸，少私寡欲. 素 is raw, undyed silk and 樸 (pǔ) is the uncarved block of wood — two of the book's signature images for the natural, unworked state, which Legge dissolves into a rhyming Victorian couplet that drops the images entirely. We restore the concrete metaphors ("the plain and undyed," "the uncarved block") because they recur across the edition and carry the chapter's argument, and we keep the two final imperatives literal: lessen the self (少私) and reduce desire (寡欲).

divergences.phrase: Give up learning, and you will have no more worries.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "When we renounce learning we have no troubles."
divergences.lectio: Give up learning, and you will have no more worries.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 絕學無憂. Legge places this line at the head of Chapter 20, and we keep it there to preserve his chapter division and segment order. Many modern scholars instead read it as the closing line of Chapter 19, where it rounds off that chapter's argument against cleverness and learning; the early texts do not mark the break, so both placements are defensible. We render 學 plainly as "learning" (book-learning, cleverness) rather than schooling in general, which is the sense the chapter goes on to disown.

divergences.phrase: like a country bumpkin
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "like a rude borderer."
divergences.lectio: I alone am awkward and useless, like a country bumpkin.
divergences.note: The Chinese 頑且鄙 describes someone stubborn, slow, and coarse — a rustic. Legge's "rude borderer" (a crude frontier-dweller) is now archaic and obscure; "country bumpkin" carries the same self-mocking sense of an unpolished simpleton, which is the tone Laozi adopts throughout the chapter as he sets his dull plainness against the crowd's brightness.

divergences.phrase: for I am nourished by the Mother, the Way
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "but I value the nursing-mother (the Tao)."
divergences.lectio: I alone am different from all the rest — for I am nourished by the Mother, the Way.
divergences.note: The Chinese 而貴食母 turns on 食 (to feed, to be fed) and 母 (mother). Legge reads it as "value the nursing-mother"; we keep both the valuing and the feeding by rendering it "nourished by the Mother," since the line's force is that Laozi, cut off from the crowd's comforts, draws his sustenance directly from the source — the Way itself, named here as the Mother who feeds all things (echoing Chapter 1's "mother of all things").

divergences.locus: opening line (孔德之容，唯道是從)
divergences.phrase: The form of great power flows from the Way alone.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The grandest forms of active force / From Tao come, their only source."
divergences.lectio: The form of great power flows from the Way alone.
divergences.note: The Chinese 孔德之容，唯道是從 says the rong (容, the look, form, or manner) of kong de (孔德, great or abundant de) follows the Way alone. De (德) is the te the book is named for — the inner power that comes of the Way, which we render "power" throughout. Legge spins it into a rhyming couplet about "the grandest forms of active force," which is faithful in spirit but buries de under abstraction. We keep it plain: great power takes its very shape from the Way and from nothing else.

divergences.locus: the essence within (其中有精；其精甚真，其中有信)
divergences.phrase: within it is an essence that is real; and this essence can be trusted
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Things' essences all there endure. / Those essences the truth enfold / Of what, when seen, shall then be told."
divergences.lectio: Deep and dark, yet within it is an essence that is real; and this essence can be trusted.
divergences.note: The crux is jing (精) and xin (信). Jing is the vital essence, the concentrated seed of life within the otherwise formless Way; the text insists qi jing shen zhen (其精甚真) — that essence is utterly real. Xin (信) is truth that can be relied on, the trust a thing keeps with you. Legge's verse turns this into essences that "enfold the truth of what, when seen, shall then be told," reading xin forward to a later disclosure and softening the bare claim. We hold the paradox the chapter is built on — the Way is elusive and vague, yet within it is an essence that is real and to be trusted — so the hidden depth and its solid core stand side by side.

divergences.locus: the origin of all things (以閱衆甫)
divergences.phrase: by it we know the origin of all things
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "So, in their beautiful array, / Things form and never know decay."
divergences.lectio: From of old until now its name has never passed away, and by it we know the origin of all things.
divergences.note: The closing turn is 自古及今，其名不去，以閱衆甫. Zhong fu (衆甫) is the beginning or father-source of the many — the origin from which all things first came. The verb yue (閱) is to review, to look through, hence to know by inspecting. Legge, following a variant, reads the line as things forming in beautiful array and never decaying, which loses the chapter's real claim: the Way's name has endured unbroken from ancient times to now, and through it we can look back to the very origin of all. We keep that thread from the deep past into the present, which sets up the final "how do I know? By this."

divergences.phrase: Yield, and remain whole.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The partial becomes complete."
divergences.lectio: Yield, and remain whole.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 曲則全. 曲 (qū) is literally "bent, crooked, curved," which Legge renders abstractly as "the partial." But the chapter's argument is practical and ethical, not geometric: it is about the strength of yielding and giving way (the same paradox as 柔弱, the soft and weak, prevailing). So we read 曲 as "yield" — to bend rather than break — which the closing line confirms by quoting this very phrase as an old proverb of self-preservation. 全 (quán) is "whole, intact, kept entire," hence "remain whole."

divergences.phrase: the sage holds to the One, and becomes a model for the world
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "the sage holds in his embrace the one thing (of humility), and manifests it to all the world."
divergences.lectio: the sage holds to the One, and becomes a model for the world
divergences.note: The Chinese is 聖人抱一為天下式. 抱一 is "embraces the One" — the One being the Way itself, the undivided unity from which all things come (cf. chapters 10, 39, 42), not narrowly "humility," which Legge supplies in brackets to fit this chapter's theme. We keep the bare "the One" and let it carry its full weight. 式 (shì) is a "pattern, standard, model" — the sage becomes a measure others can be set against — so "a model for the world" rather than Legge's "manifests it to all the world."

divergences.phrase: one who follows the Way becomes one with the Way; one who follows its power becomes one with that power; one who follows loss becomes one with loss
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "when one is making the Tao his business, those who are also pursuing it, agree with him in it, and those who are making the manifestation of its course their object agree with him in that; while even those who are failing in both these things agree with him where they fail."
divergences.lectio: So one who follows the Way becomes one with the Way; one who follows its power becomes one with that power; and one who follows loss becomes one with loss.
divergences.note: The Chinese (從事於道者，同於道；德者，同於德；失者，同於失) is a clean threefold parallel: whoever gives himself to the Way is made one with the Way, whoever to its te (power/virtue) is made one with that power, whoever to loss is made one with loss. Legge bent the lines into a sentence about people agreeing with the sage, which buries the parallel and its point — that you become whatever you devote yourself to. We restore the plain triad, the reading Walter Gorn Old (1904) and modern scholars share, and keep te as 'power' to match the rest of this edition.

divergences.phrase: A whirlwind does not last a whole morning; a downpour does not last a whole day.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day."
divergences.lectio: A whirlwind does not last a whole morning; a downpour does not last a whole day.
divergences.note: The images are kept exactly — 飄風 (the gale) and 驟雨 (the cloudburst) — since they carry the chapter's argument: even nature's most forceful acts are brief, so forced human striving is briefer still. We only trade Legge's 'violent wind' and 'sudden rain' for the tighter 'whirlwind' and 'downpour.'

divergences.phrase: leftover food and a tumor on the body
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "are like remnants of food, or a tumour on the body, which all dislike."
divergences.lectio: Seen in the light of the Way, all this is leftover food and a tumor on the body — things that everyone finds repulsive.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 餘食贅行 (yú shí zhuì xíng). Yú shí (餘食) is the scraps left over from a meal — surplus no one wants. Zhuì (贅) is a wart, a tumor, a useless growth on the body; 行 here is read as 形 (xíng, the body or form), the gloss Legge follows in rendering it "a tumour on the body." Both images say the same thing: these self-displaying acts are not virtues but excess — waste tacked onto a life, a swelling that does not belong. We keep Legge's vivid pair, since the disgust is the point: even the proud and the boastful, who think they are adding to themselves, are only piling on what everyone else wants to scrape off.

books.label: Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Way that can be spoken is not the eternal Way. The name that can be named is not the eternal name.
Nameless, it is the origin of heaven and earth. Named, it is the mother of all things.
So if you are always without desire, you see its hidden depths; but if desire is always in you, you see only its outer edges.
These two spring from the same source, though we call them by different names. Together they are the Mystery — mystery within mystery, the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.
books.title: The Way and the Name

books.label: Chapter 2
paragraphs: When everyone in the world recognizes beauty as beauty, ugliness has already appeared. When everyone recognizes good as good, what is not good has already appeared.

So it is that being and non-being give rise to each other; the difficult and the easy complete each other; the long and the short measure each other; the high and the low lean on each other; note and voice harmonize with each other; before and after follow each other. This is how it always is.
And so the sage goes about the work without forcing it, and teaches without using words.
All things arise, and the sage does not turn any away. They are brought to life, and the sage claims nothing as his own. The work is done, and he does not rest in it as an achievement.
It is just because he does not rest in it that the credit never leaves him.
books.title: The Mutual Arising of Opposites

books.label: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Do not make a show of honoring the worthy, and the people will not compete with one another. Do not prize goods that are hard to come by, and the people will not turn to theft. Do not put on display the things that stir desire, and the heart of the people will stay calm.

And so, when the sage governs, he empties their minds and fills their bellies, weakens their ambition and strengthens their bones. He keeps the people free of cunning and free of craving, so that the clever ones never dare to force their hand. Act without forcing, and nothing is left ungoverned.
books.title: Keeping the Heart Unstirred

books.label: Chapter 4
paragraphs: The Way is empty, yet however much you use it, it is never used up. It is so deep — the wellspring from which the ten thousand things flow.
It blunts the sharp edges, unties the knots, softens the glare, settles down with the dust. So still, so hidden, and yet it is always there.
I do not know whose child it is. It seems to be older than God.
books.title: The Bottomless Well

books.label: Chapter 5
paragraphs: Heaven and earth are not humane: they treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs. The sage is not humane: he treats the people as straw dogs.
The space between heaven and earth — is it not like a bellows? Empty, yet it never runs out; work it, and it gives out all the more.
Too many words run dry. Better to keep to the center.
books.title: Straw Dogs

books.label: Chapter 6
paragraphs: The valley spirit never dies. It is called the mysterious female.
The gateway of the mysterious female is called the root of heaven and earth.
Faint and unbroken, it seems always to be there; draw on it, and it is never used up.
books.title: The Valley Spirit

books.label: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Heaven lasts, and earth endures. The reason heaven and earth can last and endure is that they do not live for themselves, and so they go on living.
And so the sage puts himself last, and finds himself out in front; he sets himself aside, and so is kept safe. Is it not because he is selfless that his own self is fulfilled?
books.title: Living for No Self

books.label: Chapter 8
paragraphs: The highest good is like water. Water benefits all things and does not contend with them; it settles in the low places that everyone else scorns. And so it is close to the Way.

In where it dwells, it holds to the ground. In the heart, it holds to depth. In giving, it holds to kindness. In speech, it holds to truth. In governing, it holds to good order. In handling affairs, it holds to skill. In moving, it holds to the right moment.
It is just because it does not contend that it is without fault.
books.title: Like Water

books.label: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Keep filling a cup to the brim, and you would have done better to stop in time. Hammer a blade to its sharpest edge, and the edge will not last.
Fill your hall with gold and jade, and no one can keep them safe. Grow proud of wealth and rank, and you bring ruin on yourself.
When the work is done and your name is rising, withdraw. This is the Way of heaven.
books.title: Knowing When to Stop

books.label: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Can you hold body and soul in a single embrace and never let them part? Can you gather your breath and make it soft and supple, soft as a newborn child's? Can you cleanse the dark mirror of your mind until it is without a flaw?

Can you love the people and govern the state, and do it without scheming? When the gate of heaven opens and shuts, can you keep to the female, the yielding, receptive part? Can your understanding reach into every corner, and yet seem to know nothing at all?
To give life and to nourish it; to give life and not possess it; to do the work and not lay claim to it; to lead, and not to lord it over what you lead — this is what is called the mysterious power.
books.title: Mysterious Power

books.label: Chapter 11
paragraphs: Thirty spokes meet at a single hub, but it is the hole at the center, where there is nothing, that makes the wheel of use.
Clay is shaped into a pot, but it is the hollow inside, where there is nothing, that makes the pot of use.
Doors and windows are cut to make a room, but it is the empty space within, where there is nothing, that makes the room of use.
So what is there gives advantage; what is not there gives use.
books.title: The Use of Emptiness

books.label: Chapter 12
paragraphs: The five colors blind the eye. The five notes deafen the ear. The five flavors numb the palate. Racing and hunting drive the heart wild, and goods that are hard to come by knock a life off its course.
And so the sage goes by the belly, not the eye. He lets the one go and takes hold of the other.
books.title: The Belly, Not the Eye

books.label: Chapter 13
paragraphs: Favor and disgrace are both alarming. Honor great trouble as you honor your own body.

What does it mean that favor and disgrace are both alarming? Favor is a thing from above, and to win it is to dread losing it; to lose it is to dread something worse. This is what it means that favor and disgrace are both alarming. And what does it mean to honor great trouble as you honor your own body? The reason I can suffer great trouble is that I have a body; if I had no body, what trouble could reach me?
So the one who honors the world as their own body can be given the world to hold; the one who loves the world as their own body can be trusted with the world.
books.title: Favor and Disgrace

books.label: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Look for it, and you do not see it: call it the Unseen. Listen for it, and you do not hear it: call it the Unheard. Reach for it, and you cannot hold it: call it the Unfelt. These three cannot be pried apart and questioned one by one, so we blend them together and they are One.

Its upper side is not bright, its lower side is not dark. Unbroken, ceaseless, it cannot be named, and it returns again into nothing. This is the form of the formless, the image of what has no thing in it. This is the dim and the fleeting: meet it, and you do not see its face; follow it, and you do not see its back.
Hold fast to the ancient Way, and use it to master the things of the present. To know how things were in the beginning long ago — this is called the thread of the Way.
books.title: The Form of the Formless

books.label: Chapter 15
paragraphs: The masters of the Way in ancient times were subtle, mysterious, and deep beyond all knowing. Because they could not be known, I can only describe how they appeared.

Wary, like someone crossing a frozen stream in winter. Watchful, like someone alert to enemies on every side. Reserved, like a guest. Yielding, like ice on the point of melting. Plain, like an uncarved block of wood. Open, like a valley. And murky, like muddy water.

Who can let the muddy water settle and slowly grow clear? Who can stay still until the moment to stir? Whoever holds to this Way does not crave to be full; and because he is never full, he can wear out and be made new again.
books.title: The Ancient Masters

books.label: Chapter 16
paragraphs: Reach all the way to emptiness. Hold fast to stillness. The ten thousand things rise and stir, and I watch them return. For all their teeming growth, each one comes back to its root.

Returning to the root is stillness; this is called returning to what was fated. Returning to what was fated is the constant; to know the constant is to see clearly. Not to know it is to act blindly and bring on disaster.

Know the constant, and you grow all-embracing. All-embracing, you are impartial; impartial, you are kingly; kingly, you are like heaven; like heaven, you are one with the Way. One with the Way, you last long, and to the end of your life you come to no harm.
books.title: Returning to the Root

books.label: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The best ruler is one the people barely know is there. Next comes the ruler they love and praise. Next, the one they fear. And worst, the one they despise. Where trust runs short, it is met with distrust.
The best ruler hangs back, and is sparing of words. When the work is done and everything has run its course, the people all say: we did this ourselves.
books.title: The Best Ruler Is Barely Known

books.label: Chapter 18
paragraphs: When the great Way is abandoned, humaneness and righteousness come forward. When cleverness and sharp wits arise, great pretense follows close behind.
When the six bonds of kin fall out of harmony, filial devotion and parental love are praised. When the state sinks into disorder, loyal ministers appear.
books.title: When the Way Is Lost

books.label: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Renounce sageliness, throw out cleverness, and the people will be better off a hundredfold. Renounce humaneness, throw out righteousness, and the people will return to devotion within their families and care for one another. Renounce ingenuity, throw out the chase after gain, and there will be no more thieves or bandits.
These three are mere ornament, and ornament is not enough. So let the people hold to something solid: see the plain and undyed, hold to the uncarved block, think little of self, and want little.
books.title: Return to the Uncarved Block

books.label: Chapter 20
paragraphs: Give up learning, and you will have no more worries. Between a respectful "yes" and a careless "yeah," how much difference is there really? Between what people call good and what they call bad, how wide is the gulf that separates them?
What everyone fears must indeed be feared. But how vast and endless this all is, with no place to come to rest!

The crowd is merry and content, as if feasting at a great banquet, as if climbing a tower in spring. I alone am still, giving no sign, my desires not yet stirring, like an infant that has not yet learned to smile. I am weary and forlorn, like one with no home to return to. Everyone else has more than enough; I alone seem to have lost everything. Mine is the mind of a fool, muddled and dim.

Ordinary people are bright and clever; I alone am dull. Ordinary people are sharp and sure; I alone am clouded and confused. I drift like the restless sea; I am blown about, as if I had nowhere to settle. Everyone else has their work and their purpose; I alone am awkward and useless, like a country bumpkin. I alone am different from all the rest — for I am nourished by the Mother, the Way.
books.title: Alone and Adrift

books.label: Chapter 21
paragraphs: The form of great power flows from the Way alone.

And the Way itself, as a thing, is elusive and vague. Vague and elusive, yet within it are images. Elusive and vague, yet within it are things. Deep and dark, yet within it is an essence that is real; and this essence can be trusted.
From of old until now its name has never passed away, and by it we know the origin of all things. How do I know the way of all things at their origin? By this.
books.title: The Essence Within

books.label: Chapter 22
paragraphs: Yield, and remain whole. Bend, and stay straight. Empty yourself, and be filled. Wear out, and be made new. Have little, and you will gain; have much, and you will be confused.

And so the sage holds to the One, and becomes a model for the world. He does not display himself, and so he shines. He does not justify himself, and so he is known. He does not boast, and so he is given credit. He is not proud, and so he endures. It is because he does not contend that no one in the world can contend with him.
The old saying — yield, and remain whole — how could that be empty words? Truly it keeps a person whole, and brings them home.
books.title: Yield and Remain Whole

books.label: Chapter 23
paragraphs: To say little is the way of nature. A whirlwind does not last a whole morning; a downpour does not last a whole day. Who makes these things? Heaven and earth. And if even heaven and earth cannot make them last long, how much less can a person.
So one who follows the Way becomes one with the Way; one who follows its power becomes one with that power; and one who follows loss becomes one with loss.

The Way gladly receives whoever becomes one with the Way; its power gladly receives whoever becomes one with that power; and loss gladly receives whoever becomes one with loss. Where there is not trust enough, no trust is returned.
books.title: Few Words Are Natural

books.label: Chapter 24
paragraphs: Stand on tiptoe, and you cannot keep your balance. Take great striding steps, and you cannot keep walking.

Show yourself off, and you do not shine. Insist you are right, and you are not seen for what you are. Boast of what you have done, and the credit is not given you. Be proud of yourself, and you do not last.
Seen in the light of the Way, all this is leftover food and a tumor on the body — things that everyone finds repulsive. And so whoever holds to the Way will have nothing to do with them.
books.title: Standing on Tiptoe
